_comment: Hand-authored anchors for places the two inputs miss. Natural Earth's populated-places file is ranked by modern prominence, so an island whose whole significance is that almost nobody lives there never clears the cut, and the legacy extraction did not cover the open Pacific at all. Coordinates are the main settlement or the island's centre, taken from the source named in `why`. Fields left out are filled by the same defaults and coast/river search as every other record.

places.name: Po Valley
places.why: The Po Valley is in northern Italy; the short name Po also names an unrelated place in West Africa.

places.name: Orkney
places.why: Continuously settled from the fourth millennium BCE — Skara Brae, Maeshowe, the Ness of Brodgar — then a Pictish province, then the seat of a Norse earldom, and Scottish only from 1468. The default climate rule made it boreal, which is wrong for a treeless oceanic archipelago.

places.name: Faroe Islands
places.why: The middle leg of the North Atlantic crossing, with barley and sheep from the sixth century CE. With Orkney added, the whole Norse route — Orkney, Faroes, Iceland, Greenland — is now on the map.

places.name: Rapa Nui
places.why: The most isolated inhabited place on Earth, and the point of the simulation is to be able to stand in one. The longitude rule would otherwise have filed it as South American.

places.name: Marquesas Islands
places.why: The dispersal hearth for East Polynesia: Hawaii, Rapa Nui and probably New Zealand were settled from here. Nothing at all stood between 120°W and 105°W south of the equator.

places.name: Socotra
places.why: A monsoon-trade waypoint named in the Periplus, with a Greek-speaking community, then a Christian one, and a flora found nowhere else. The default climate rule called it tropical on latitude alone.

places.name: Chatham Islands
places.why: The far southeastern edge of Polynesian settlement, where the Moriori gave up horticulture for a maritime forager economy because nothing they brought would grow. The anchor is the island's interior rather than Waitangi on the west coast: at atlas resolution the shore reads as open water.

places.name: Pohnpei
places.why: Nan Madol — a city of ninety-odd artificial islets walled in basalt logs, begun around 1200 CE — is the largest thing anyone built in the Pacific, and Micronesia had almost nothing between the Marshalls and the Philippines. Chosen over Tarawa because the atlas coastline has no atoll there, so a Tarawa anchor would have generated in open water. The longitude rule would otherwise have filed it as Southeast Asian.

places.name: Kilwa
places.why: The richest Swahili port in the fourteenth century, which controlled the gold trade from Sofala; Ibn Battuta visited in 1331.

places.name: Great Zimbabwe
places.why: Capital of a Shona state of perhaps ten thousand people between about 1100 and 1450, built in dry-stone enclosures.

places.name: Mapungubwe
places.why: Hilltop capital at the Limpopo-Shashe confluence, about 1075-1220, the forerunner of Great Zimbabwe.

places.name: Aksum
places.why: Royal town of the Aksumite kingdom from the first century CE, which minted coins and adopted Christianity under Ezana about 340.

places.name: Lalibela
places.why: Zagwe royal centre whose rock-hewn churches were cut around 1200.

places.name: Lamu
places.why: A Swahili stone town continuously inhabited since the fourteenth century.

places.name: Meroë
places.why: Capital of the kingdom of Kush from about 590 BCE to 350 CE, with iron smelting and its own pyramids. Filed with the Nile valley.

places.name: Koumbi Saleh
places.why: Probably the capital of ancient Ghana that al-Bakri described in 1068, with a Muslim merchant town and a royal town.

places.name: Ile-Ife
places.why: Sacred city of the Yoruba, known for naturalistic brass and terracotta heads of about 1200-1400.

places.name: Mbanza Kongo
places.why: Capital of the kingdom of Kongo, where Afonso I ruled as a Christian king from 1509.

places.name: Cahokia
places.why: The largest town north of Mexico, about 1050-1250, with Monks Mound and perhaps ten to twenty thousand people.

places.name: Chaco Canyon
places.why: Great houses such as Pueblo Bonito were built here from about 850 to 1150, linked by roads across the San Juan basin.

places.name: Teotihuacan
places.why: A city of perhaps a hundred thousand at its height around 450 CE, laid out on the Avenue of the Dead.

places.name: Monte Albán
places.why: Zapotec capital on a levelled mountaintop above the Oaxaca valley, about 500 BCE to 750 CE.

places.name: Chichén Itzá
places.why: The dominant city of the northern Yucatán from about 900 to 1100.

places.name: Chan Chan
places.why: Capital of the Chimú kingdom, built of adobe compounds on the desert coast until the Inca conquest about 1470.

places.name: Huacas de Moche
places.why: The Moche ceremonial capital of about 100-800 CE, with the Huaca del Sol, one of the largest adobe structures in the Americas.

places.name: Caral
places.why: Platform mounds and sunken plazas from about 2600 BCE, among the oldest towns in the Americas.

places.name: Huari
places.why: Capital of the Wari state, about 600-1000, in the Ayacucho valley.

places.name: Tiwanaku
places.why: Ceremonial city near Lake Titicaca, about 500-1000, fed by raised fields at 3,800 metres.

places.name: Tongatapu
places.why: Seat of the Tu'i Tonga, whose maritime chiefdom reached Samoa and 'Uvea; the royal tombs at Lapaha date from about 1200.

places.name: Kealakekua Bay
places.why: A chiefly centre on the Kona coast of Hawai'i island, with the heiau of Hikiau, where Cook landed in 1779.

places.name: Guovdageaidnu
places.why: A Sámi reindeer-herding centre of the Finnmark plateau. The gazetteer has no Sámi place, and Tromsø is a Norwegian town.

places.name: Jokkmokk
places.why: Lule Sámi winter market site since 1605.

places.name: Angkor
places.why: The Khmer capital from the ninth to the fifteenth century, with reservoirs and canals around Angkor Wat and Angkor Thom.

places.name: Ayutthaya
places.why: Siamese capital from 1351 until its sack in 1767, on an island in the Chao Phraya.

places.name: Melaka
places.why: The sultanate that controlled the strait from about 1400 until the Portuguese took it in 1511.

places.name: Trowulan
places.why: Capital of Majapahit, the fourteenth-century Javanese empire, built in fired brick.

places.name: Hormuz
places.why: The island entrepot that controlled Gulf trade from about 1300 until 1622.

places.name: Vijayanagara
places.why: Capital of the Vijayanagara empire, perhaps the second-largest city in the world about 1500, sacked in 1565.

places.name: Persepolis
places.why: Ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid kings from about 518 BCE until Alexander burned it in 330.

places.name: Ctesiphon
places.why: Parthian and Sasanian capital on the Tigris until the Arab conquest of 637.

places.name: Merv
places.why: Seljuk capital of Khorasan and one of the largest cities in the world before the Mongols destroyed it in 1221.

places.name: Sarai
places.why: Capital of the Golden Horde on the lower Volga in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries.

places.name: Novgorod
places.why: Merchant republic of the north, with log-paved streets and birch-bark letters, independent until 1478.

places.name: Constantinople
places.why: Capital of the eastern Roman empire from 330 until the Ottoman conquest in 1453. The gazetteer's Istanbul entry is the modern city.

places.name: Gyeongju
places.why: The Silla capital for nearly a thousand years, laid out in grid wards on the Tang model.

places.name: Kaesong
places.why: Capital of Goryeo from 919 to 1392.
